messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Amir is a 27-year-old physical therapist, married for three years, who was sexually assaulted two years ago by a male acquaintance at a party. That night, the man wore a heavy, sweet cologne, and during the assault Amir experienced sharp pain in his lower back and pelvis—sensations he still recalls with visceral clarity. The scent, the physical hurt, and the utter loss of control fused into a single unbearable memory. In the months afterward, Amir struggled to push the event out of his mind, but it kept resurfacing. He began to notice that whenever a patient came in wearing a similar cologne, the smell would hit him before he even saw them, and the feeling of shame about what happened to his body would surge up—that his body had been violated and was now permanently marked. He came to believe that he would never be able to feel normal emotions again, that something essential in him had been broken, and that he could no longer rely on himself to stay safe. That belief in his own unreliability made him hypervigilant: he started scanning his environment for unexpected movement and reacting with alarm when someone touched him, even a light tap on the shoulder from a colleague during a consultation.

The more ashamed he felt of his body, the more sensitive he became to physical pain—his own and others’. While treating a patient’s muscle strain, he would notice a twinge in his own back and immediately feel a rush of the same body shame, which then intensified his startle response. Even the gentle brush of his wife’s hand at night could make him flinch, and he would dissociate, pretending it was happening to someone else. This dazed detachment during intimacy only deepened his shame and fed the cycle—avoiding the thought of the assault meant he never processed it, so the threat remained raw, and the smallest sensory reminder triggered a cascade of alarm. He began to monitor his body constantly, checking for any sign of injury or danger, and this hyperawareness made him more likely to notice subtle pains and more prone to being startled by them. At work, a patient’s unexpected movement during an exercise routine could make him jump, and he would then feel even less able to trust himself, reinforcing his belief that he couldn’t rely on his own reactions.

Over the past year, Amir’s avoidance strategies have taken a toll. He avoids thinking about the assault during the day, but at night he lies rigidly in bed, listening for sounds that aren’t there, hyperalert to his wife’s breathing. He has started canceling evening plans with friends because he cannot tolerate being close to anyone after dark. His marriage has become strained; his wife feels he is distant and that intimacy is fraught with tension. What finally brought him to therapy was a single moment: last month, during a session with a patient who wore the same cologne, Amir froze, dissociated completely, and could not finish the treatment. He knew then that he could no longer rely on his old strategies. He is terrified that he will never regain his sense of self or his capacity for closeness, but he also hopes that by finally talking about the assault he might stop living in a constant state of alarm.
